questions.stem: One word for: 'A person who hates women'

options.option_text: Misogynist (correct: miso=hate, gyn=woman; misogynist = one who hates women ✓)
Misanthropist (wrong: misanthropist = one who hates ALL people, not specifically women)
Chauvinist (wrong: chauvinist = person who believes their group is superior; a male chauvinist demeanes women but it's not the precise term for 'hates women')
Philogynist (wrong: philogynist = one who loves women — exact opposite)

questions.explanation: A is correct. MISOGYNIST = someone who hates, dislikes, or is strongly prejudiced against women. From Greek: misos (hatred) + gynē (woman). Related: misogyny (noun), misogynistic (adjective). Contrast: misandrist (hates men), misanthropist (hates all humans), philogynist (loves women).

questions.stem: One word for: 'Government by the few'

options.option_text: Democracy (wrong: democracy = government by the many/people)
Oligarchy (correct: oligos=few, archein=to rule; oligarchy = rule by a small group ✓)
Aristocracy (wrong: aristocracy = rule by the 'best' or nobility — a type of few but specifically elite)
Monarchy (wrong: monarchy = rule by one person/monarch)

questions.explanation: B is correct. OLIGARCHY = government by a small group. From Greek: oligos (few) + archein (to rule). Oligarchs control massive wealth and power. Examples: Russia (oligarchs), some historical city-states. Compare: monarchy (1), oligarchy (few), democracy (many), plutocracy (wealthy few).

questions.stem: One word for: 'Fear of open spaces or public places'

options.option_text: Claustrophobia (wrong: claustrophobia = fear of ENCLOSED spaces — opposite)
Agoraphobia (correct: agora=marketplace/public place; agoraphobia = fear of open/public spaces ✓)
Xenophobia (wrong: xenophobia = fear or hatred of strangers/foreigners)
Acrophobia (wrong: acrophobia = fear of heights)

questions.explanation: B is correct. AGORAPHOBIA = fear of open spaces, public places, or situations where escape might be difficult. From Greek: agora (marketplace) + phobos (fear). CLAUSTROPHOBIA = fear of enclosed spaces (opposite). Common -phobia words: acrophobia (heights), arachnophobia (spiders), hydrophobia (water), xenophobia (foreigners).

questions.stem: One word for: 'A speech delivered to oneself (as if no one is listening)'

options.option_text: Dialogue (wrong: dialogue = conversation between two or more people)
Soliloquy (correct: sol=alone, loqui=to speak; soliloquy = speaking to oneself ✓)
Monologue (wrong: monologue = a long speech by one person but to an audience)
Eulogy (wrong: eulogy = speech of praise, especially for a deceased person)

questions.explanation: B is correct. SOLILOQUY = the act of speaking one's thoughts aloud when alone or regardless of any hearers. Famous in drama (Hamlet's 'To be or not to be'). From Latin: solus (alone) + loqui (to speak). MONOLOGUE = extended speech to an audience. DIALOGUE = between two+ people. EULOGY = speech praising the dead.

questions.stem: One word for: 'A doctor who treats the diseases of the eye'

options.option_text: Optometrist (wrong: optometrist measures vision/eyesight and prescribes glasses but is NOT a medical doctor)
Ophthalmologist (correct: ophthalmos=eye; ophthalmologist = a medical doctor specialising in eye diseases ✓)
Optician (wrong: optician makes and fits glasses/contact lenses — not a doctor)
Neurologist (wrong: neurologist treats the nervous system, not specifically the eyes)

questions.explanation: B is correct. OPHTHALMOLOGIST = a medical doctor who specialises in diagnosing and treating diseases and conditions of the eye (including surgery). OPTOMETRIST = tests vision, prescribes glasses (not a medical doctor). OPTICIAN = makes/dispenses glasses. The hierarchy: Ophthalmologist (MD) > Optometrist (OD) > Optician.

questions.stem: One word for: 'The study of coins and medals'

options.option_text: Philately (wrong: philately = the collection/study of stamps)
Numismatics (correct: numisma=coin; numismatics = study/collection of coins and medals ✓)
Cartography (wrong: cartography = the science/art of making maps)
Calligraphy (wrong: calligraphy = the art of beautiful handwriting)

questions.explanation: B is correct. NUMISMATICS = the study or collection of currency, including coins, paper money, and medals. A numismatist = coin collector. Related -atics words: philately (stamps), cartography (maps), typography (printing/fonts), calligraphy (handwriting).

questions.stem: One word for: 'A person who believes that pleasure is the highest good'

options.option_text: Stoic (wrong: a stoic endures pain/hardship without complaint — opposite approach to pleasure)
Hedonist (correct: hedone=pleasure; hedonist = one who believes pleasure is life's chief goal ✓)
Nihilist (wrong: nihilist = one who believes life has no meaning or value)
Pragmatist (wrong: pragmatist = one who is practical and result-oriented)

questions.explanation: B is correct. HEDONIST = a person who believes that the pursuit of pleasure is the most important thing in life. From Greek: hedone (pleasure). Hedonism = the ethical theory that pleasure is the highest good. STOIC (endures hardship), EPICUREAN (moderate pleasure), ASCETIC (self-denial) are contrasting philosophical stances.

questions.stem: One word for: 'Words inscribed on a tomb'

options.option_text: Epitaph (correct: epi=upon, taphos=tomb; epitaph = inscription written on a grave ✓)
Epigraph (wrong: epigraph = a motto or quotation at the beginning of a literary work)
Epilogue (wrong: epilogue = a concluding section of a book/play)
Elegy (wrong: elegy = a mournful poem, especially for the dead — a poem, not an inscription)

questions.explanation: A is correct. EPITAPH = an inscription on a tomb or gravestone, usually in memory of the person buried there. From Greek: epi (upon) + taphos (tomb). Famous epitaph example: 'Rest in Peace.' Confused with: EPIGRAPH (motto in a book), ELEGY (poem of mourning), EULOGY (speech praising the dead).

questions.stem: One word for: 'A person who sells flowers'

options.option_text: Florist (correct: florist = a person who sells flowers and makes floral arrangements ✓)
Botanist (wrong: botanist = a scientist who studies plants)
Horticulturist (wrong: horticulturist = one who cultivates gardens; not specifically a flower seller)
Nurseryman (wrong: nurseryman grows and sells plants/seedlings; not specifically flowers)

questions.explanation: A is correct. FLORIST = a person who sells flowers and plants and makes floral arrangements. From Latin: flos/floris (flower). Related: flora (plant life), floral (relating to flowers). Compare: botanist (studies plants scientifically), horticulturist (grows gardens), nurseryman (grows plants for sale).

questions.stem: One word for: 'A collection of maps'

options.option_text: Directory (wrong: directory = a book listing names, addresses, or information)
Atlas (correct: atlas = a book of maps; named after the Titan Atlas who held up the heavens ✓)
Almanac (wrong: almanac = an annual publication with data, weather forecasts, and astronomical information)
Gazetteer (wrong: gazetteer = a geographical dictionary or index — lists place names)

questions.explanation: B is correct. ATLAS = a book or collection of maps. Named after Atlas, the Greek Titan who bore the heavens on his shoulders (16th-century mapmaker Gerard Mercator used an image of Atlas on his map collection's frontispiece). Gazetteer = geographical index; almanac = annual reference book; directory = address/information list.
